name: Southwest Route / Icy Glacier
approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (Trail #674) at road's end on FS Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road), off SR 542 (Mt. Baker Highway), elevation ~3,100 ft. Hike Trail #674 roughly 4 miles, switchbacking up through forest along Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft), gaining ~2,000 ft. The signed Hannegan Camp (~3.5 mi in) is the last reliable water on the trail — fill up there, as there is no running water past it for the rest of the route. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and go cross-country east/northeast, climbing open heather meadows and scattered timber onto Ruth Mountain's north side (3rd-class terrain through trees in spots), then rope up and ascend the moderate slopes of the Ruth Glacier — crevasses open up here in late season, especially on the upper mountain — to Ruth Mountain's summit (7,115 ft). Most parties treat this as a 5–6 hour trailhead-to-camp day, camping on Ruth's summit plateau or in the saddle beyond it. From camp, descend Ruth's south/west side about 1,400 ft from the summit (about 900 ft from the notch camp); there are two common lines down — a steep, loose gully some parties call the 'death gully,' or safer heather slopes and a game trail on climber's left (2nd–3rd class) — down to the Ruth–Icy saddle (~5,700 ft). From the saddle, traverse talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the Icy Glacier, rope up again, and climb the glacier's northwest slope gradually southeast, keeping the rock ridge on your left and crevasses on your right, to about 6,500 ft. Traverse the upper glacier below Icy's west face, skirting the west notch (watch for a bergschrund near the top some seasons), to reach a notch/saddle west of Icy's Northwest Spire (~6,500 ft). From there climb roughly 500 ft of 2nd–3rd class talus and snow up Icy's south side to the base of a light-colored, ~100-ft 4th-class summit gully with solid jugs and ledges; this leads to the northwest summit. Note the true high point is a separate southeast tower about 11 ft higher, reached by additional 3rd/4th class scrambling — many parties only tag the northwest summit, which holds the register. Hazards throughout: crevasses on both the Ruth and Icy Glaciers, occasional rockfall on Icy's south-side scramble terrain, black flies and mosquitoes on the lower trail in summer, and essentially no water source after Hannegan Camp. A few moves in the summit gully feel low-fifth class rather than straightforward 4th class, depending on the exact line chosen.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, over Ruth Mountain, then the Icy Glacier's northwest slope to the west notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at road's end on FS Road 32, near 3,100 ft, hike Trail #674 roughly four miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft. Hannegan Camp about 3.5 miles in is the last reliable water on the route — fill up there, because there is nothing running past it.

From the pass go cross-country east and northeast up heather meadows and scattered timber onto Ruth's north side, with some third-class ground through trees, then rope up for the Ruth Glacier to Ruth's summit at 7,115 ft. Most parties treat trailhead-to-camp as a five to six hour day and camp on Ruth's summit plateau or in the saddle beyond.

From camp, descend Ruth's south and west side about 1,400 ft from the summit (about 900 ft from the notch camp) to the Ruth-Icy saddle near 5,700 ft, taking the heather slopes and game trail on climber's left rather than the steep loose gully. From the saddle, traverse talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the Icy Glacier.
hazards: No water source at all after Hannegan Camp
Crevasses on both the Ruth and the Icy Glaciers, and a bergschrund near the west notch in some seasons
Loose rock in the summit gully with the whole party funnelled through it — helmets are standard
The steep loose 'death gully' off Ruth, which is the natural fall line and the wrong option
Roughly 1,400 ft of regain from the Ruth-Icy saddle over Ruth on the way home
approach_variants.baseFinding:
On the Icy Glacier, keep the rock ridge on your left and the crevasses on your right. That is the navigation instruction for the whole glacier and it works without seeing the summit: climb the northwest slope gradually southeast to about 6,500 ft with a rock ridge as your left-hand handrail. If the rock swings round to your right, you have crossed the glacier and are heading for the wrong side of the peak.

The notch is the base, and it is west of the Northwest Spire at roughly 6,500 ft. Traverse the upper glacier below Icy's west face, skirting the west notch — some seasons there is a bergschrund near the top of it — to reach the notch or saddle just west of the Northwest Spire.

There is a long horizontal crevasse near the top of the glacier, right below the Icy towers, and it is a useful landmark rather than only a hazard: it runs across your line just where the glacier ends beneath the peak. Meeting it means you are at the top of the glacier.

The climbing starts at the first prominent gully. From the notch, about 500 ft of second and third class talus and snow up Icy's south side reaches the base of a light-coloured, roughly 100 ft fourth-class gully on the left, with solid jugs and ledges. There are rappel slings around a horn at its top, left by previous parties. Colour, length and the slings at the top are three independent confirmations, which is more than most gullies in the Cascades offer.

Which summit: the gully leads to the northwest summit, which holds the register. The true high point is a separate southeast tower about 11 ft higher, reached by more third and fourth class scrambling. Many parties only tag the northwest one — decide in advance rather than at the notch.

A few moves in the gully feel low fifth rather than fourth, depending on the exact line taken. That is not a sign you are off route; it is the route.
